topics.title: Money as a medium of exchange

concepts.label: Money as a Medium of Exchange
concepts.cardText: A person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service. Without money, a shoe manufacturer who wants wheat would have to find a farmer who both sells wheat and wants to buy shoes: both parties must agree to sell and buy each other's commodities. This is the double coincidence of wants, an essential feature of a barter system. Money provides the crucial intermediate step and eliminates the need for it: the shoe manufacturer only needs a buyer for his shoes. Since money acts as an intermediate in exchange, it is called a medium of exchange.
concepts.hint: What does the shoe manufacturer need to find if there is no money? What changes with money?
concepts.probe: How does money solve the problem of double coincidence of wants? Explain with an example.
concepts.causeChain: Barter needs double coincidence of wants (each must want what the other sells) -> hard to find -> money acts as an intermediate -> sell goods for money, buy anything with money -> money is a medium of exchange

causeLinks.criterion: Connects money acting as an intermediate in exchange to eliminating the need for a double coincidence of wants.

keyPoints.text: Without money, a shoe manufacturer who wants wheat would have to look for a wheat growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat but also wants to buy the shoes in exchange. Both parties have to agree to sell and buy each others commodities. This is known as double coincidence of wants. In a barter system where goods are directly exchanged without the use of money, double coincidence of wants is an essential feature.
keyPoints.followUp: What problem would a shoe maker who wants wheat face if there were no money?

checks.criterion: Explains double coincidence of wants: both parties must want to sell and buy each other's goods, which is an essential feature of barter.

keyPoints.text: In an economy where money is in use, money by providing the crucial intermediate step eliminates the need for double coincidence of wants. The shoe manufacturer only has to find a buyer for his shoes; once he has exchanged his shoes for money, he can purchase wheat or any other commodity. Since money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, it is called a medium of exchange.
keyPoints.followUp: How does money get rid of that problem?

checks.criterion: Explains that money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, eliminating the need for double coincidence of wants, and so is called a medium of exchange.

concepts.label: Currency as Money
concepts.cardText: Before coins, Indians used grains and cattle as money, then gold, silver and copper coins. Modern currency, paper notes and coins, is not made of precious metal and has no use of its own. It is accepted as a medium of exchange because it is authorised by the government. In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, and no other individual or organisation may issue currency. The law makes the rupee a medium of payment that cannot be refused in India, so the rupee is widely accepted.

concepts.label: Demand Deposits and Cheques
concepts.cardText: People deposit extra cash with banks, which keep it safe and pay interest. Since these deposits can be withdrawn on demand, they are called demand deposits. A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person's account to the person named on it, so payments can be settled without cash, as when M. Salim pays his leather supplier. Since demand deposits are widely accepted as a means of payment, along with currency, they constitute money in the modern economy. Modern forms of money are closely linked to the banking system.

keyPoints.text: People deposit extra cash with the banks by opening a bank account. Banks accept the deposits and also pay an amount as interest. People's money is safe with the banks and earns interest, and people can withdraw it as and when they require. Since the deposits in the bank accounts can be withdrawn on demand, these deposits are called demand deposits.

concepts.label: Loan Activities of Banks
concepts.cardText: Banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash, about 5 per cent in India these days, to pay depositors who withdraw money on any day; since only some depositors come on a given day, this is enough. Banks use the major portion of deposits to extend loans. In this way, banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (depositors) and those who need funds (borrowers). Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits, and this difference is their main source of income.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects banks needing only a small cash reserve (since few depositors withdraw on any day) to their using most deposits to give loans.

keyPoints.text: Banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash with themselves; banks in India these days hold about 5 per cent of their deposits as cash. concepts.label: Credit: Positive Role and Debt-Trap
concepts.cardText: Credit (loan) is an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment. Salim, a shoe manufacturer, borrows to meet the working capital needs of a festival order, delivers on time, makes a profit and repays: credit plays a vital and positive role. Swapna, a small farmer, borrows from a moneylender for groundnut, but pests destroy her crop; the debt grows and she must sell part of her land. This is a debt-trap. Whether credit is useful depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is support in case of loss.
concepts.hint: Both Salim and Swapna borrowed. Why did one gain and the other lose land?
concepts.probe: How can credit help one borrower but push another into a debt-trap?
concepts.causeChain: Credit meets working capital needs -> production on time -> higher earnings (Salim); but crop failure -> loan cannot be repaid -> debt grows -> land sold (Swapna's debt-trap) -> usefulness of credit depends on risk and support

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the risk of crop failure (with no support) to credit pushing the borrower into a debt-trap.

keyPoints.text: Credit (loan) refers to an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment.

checks.criterion: Explains how credit helped Salim meet working capital needs, complete production on time and increase earnings: a positive role.

Credit, instead of helping her improve her earnings, left her worse off. This is commonly called debt-trap: credit pushes the borrower into a situation from which recovery is very painful.

concepts.label: Terms of Credit and Collateral
concepts.cardText: Every loan agreement specifies an interest rate that the borrower pays along with repaying the principal. Lenders may also demand collateral: an asset the borrower owns, such as land, a building, a vehicle, livestock or bank deposits, used as a guarantee until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender can sell the collateral. Megha's Rs 5 lakh housing loan at 12 per cent, repaid in monthly instalments over 10 years, needed salary documents and the house papers as collateral. Interest rate, collateral and documentation, and the mode of repayment together are the terms of credit, which vary between lenders and borrowers.

concepts.label: Variety of Credit Arrangements in Sonpur
concepts.cardText: In Sonpur, Shyamal, a small farmer, once borrowed from a moneylender at 5 per cent a month (60 per cent a year) and now borrows from a trader at 3 per cent a month, but must sell his crop to the trader, who buys it cheaply after harvest. Arun, with seven acres, gets a bank loan at 8.5 per cent a year. Rama, a landless labourer, borrows from her employer at 5 per cent a month and repays by working for him; the only source of credit for the landless is the landowner-employers. Cooperatives, like the Krishak Cooperative, are the other major source of cheap rural credit: members pool resources, and their deposits serve as collateral for a large bank loan.

concepts.label: Formal and Informal Sources of Credit
concepts.cardText: Loans can be grouped as formal sector loans (from banks and cooperatives) and informal sector loans (from moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends). The Reserve Bank of India supervises formal lenders: it checks that banks maintain a minimum cash balance and lend not just to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators and small borrowers, and banks report their lending to it. No organisation supervises informal lenders: they can charge any interest and use unfair means to recover money. Their much higher interest takes a larger part of borrowers' earnings and can lead to a debt-trap. Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects informal lenders having no supervision to their charging much higher interest, which raises the cost of borrowing and can cause a debt-trap.

Banks periodically submit information to the RBI on how much they lend, to whom, and at what interest rate.

Most informal lenders charge a much higher interest on loans, so a larger part of borrowers' earnings is used to repay the loan, which can lead to increasing debt and debt trap, and discourage people from starting enterprises.

concepts.label: Formal and Informal Credit: Who Gets What?
concepts.cardText: In urban areas, 54 per cent of loans taken by poor households come from informal sources, while rich households take only 17 per cent from informal and 83 per cent from formal sources; the pattern is similar in rural areas. The rich get cheap formal credit while the poor pay a lot to borrow. The formal sector still meets only about half of rural people's credit needs. So banks and cooperatives must increase their lending, especially in rural areas, and formal credit must be distributed more equally so the poor can benefit from cheaper loans.

concepts.causeChain: Rich households get most loans from cheap formal sources; poor depend on costly informal sources -> formal sector meets only about half of rural needs -> banks and cooperatives must lend more, and more equally, to the poor

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the poor depending on costly informal credit to the need to expand formal credit and distribute it more equally.

keyPoints.text: 54 per cent of the loans taken by poor households in the urban areas are from informal sources. Only 17 per cent of rich urban households' loans are from informal sources, while 83 per cent are from formal sources. A similar pattern is found in rural areas. The rich households are availing cheap credit from formal lenders whereas the poor households have to pay a large amount for borrowing.
keyPoints.followUp: How do poorer and better-off households differ in where they get their loans?

checks.criterion: States that poor households depend mostly on informal sources while rich households get most of their credit from cheap formal sources (for example 54 per cent versus 17 per cent informal in urban areas).

keyPoints.text: The formal sector still meets only about half of the total credit needs of the rural people. It is necessary that banks and cooperatives increase their lending particularly in the rural areas, so that the dependence on informal sources of credit reduces. It is also important that formal credit is distributed more equally so that the poor can benefit from the cheaper loans.
keyPoints.followUp: How much of rural people's credit needs does the formal sector meet, and what should change?

concepts.label: Self Help Groups for the Poor
concepts.cardText: Banks are not present everywhere, and bank loans need documents and collateral; absence of collateral is a major reason the poor cannot get bank loans. Moneylenders lend without collateral but charge very high interest, keep no records and harass borrowers. Self Help Groups organise the rural poor, especially women, into groups of 15-20 who save regularly (Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more) and take small loans from the group at less than moneylenders' rates. After a year or two of regular saving, the group can get a bank loan in its name. The group decides on loans and is responsible for repayment, so banks lend without collateral. SHGs help women become financially self-reliant and discuss social issues.
concepts.hint: Why will a bank lend to a group of poor women when it would not lend to any one of them alone?
concepts.probe: What is the basic idea behind Self Help Groups, and how do they help the poor overcome the problem of collateral?
concepts.causeChain: Poor lack collateral -> no bank loans -> depend on costly moneylenders; SHG: members save together, group decides and is responsible for repayment -> banks lend to the group without collateral -> timely loans at reasonable interest

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the group being responsible for repayment to banks being willing to lend to SHGs without collateral.

keyPoints.text: Banks are not present everywhere in rural India, and bank loans require proper documents and collateral. Absence of collateral is one of the major reasons which prevents the poor from getting bank loans. Moneylenders know the borrowers personally and lend without collateral, but they charge very high rates of interest, keep no records of the transactions and harass the poor borrowers.
keyPoints.followUp: Why is it hard for poor people to get loans from banks?

checks.criterion: Explains that the poor cannot get bank loans mainly because they lack collateral (and documents), so they depend on moneylenders who charge very high interest.

keyPoints.text: The idea is to organise rural poor, in particular women, into small Self Help Groups (SHGs) and pool (collect) their savings. A typical SHG has 15-20 members, usually from one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly. Members can take small loans from the group itself at interest less than what the moneylender charges. After a year or two of regular saving, the group becomes eligible for a bank loan, sanctioned in the name of the group, meant to create self-employment opportunities.
keyPoints.followUp: How is a Self Help Group organised, and how does it work?

checks.criterion: Explains the basic idea of SHGs: organising the rural poor, especially women, into small groups that pool their savings and lend to members.
Mentions that after a year or two of regular saving, the group becomes eligible for a bank loan in its name, for self-employment.

keyPoints.text: Most of the important decisions regarding the savings and loan activities are taken by the group members, including the purpose, amount, interest and repayment schedule. It is the group which is responsible for the repayment of the loan; non-repayment by any member is followed up seriously by the others. Because of this, banks are willing to lend to poor women organised in SHGs, even though they have no collateral. Thus SHGs help borrowers overcome the problem of lack of collateral.
keyPoints.followUp: Who takes decisions in a Self Help Group, and how does that solve the problem of security for loans?

requiredEvidence: overcome the problem of lack of collateral

checks.criterion: States that the group members take the decisions and the group is responsible for repayment of the loan.
Explains that SHGs help borrowers overcome the lack of collateral, since banks lend to the group without it.

keyPoints.text: SHGs are the building blocks of organisation of the rural poor. They help women become financially self-reliant, and regular meetings provide a platform to discuss and act on social issues such as health, nutrition and domestic violence.

checks.criterion: Mentions that SHGs help women become financially self-reliant and give a platform to discuss social issues like health, nutrition or domestic violence.

keyPoints.text: Grameen Bank of Bangladesh is one of the biggest success stories in reaching the poor to meet their credit needs at reasonable rates. Started in the 1970s, in 2018 it had over 9 million members in about 81,600 villages. Almost all borrowers are women from the poorest sections, who have proved to be reliable borrowers. Its founder, Professor Muhammad Yunus, received the 2006 Nobel Prize for Peace.

checks.criterion: Gives the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh as an example of reaching poor women with credit at reasonable rates (founded by Muhammad Yunus).
